APPLICATION Submissions by MR MYERS
Yes, Mr Myers.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord, we're grateful for the time this morning just to prepare to start the submission. The court knows that we make a submission of no case to answer and I'll set out the parameters of that shortly.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Your Lordship will have the defence submission and bundle --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: -- the prosecution response, for which we are grateful. We appreciate that has been dealt with in quite a short compass of time, we understand that, inevitably.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: There were two authorities that I sent through to your Lordship, but I'm grateful to Mr Maher, who's actually dealing with the printing of them --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Well, I gather that my clerk said could he print them off but I don't think they need to be because you're only referring to discrete paragraphs --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It is --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So don't print the whole thing off.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: And it's only to support a proposition that I put to the court that in its basic terms, I anticipate, is not controversial. It's a matter of applicability to the current situation. They are authorities, the general circumstances of which the court will be aware of.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Can someone stop him printing off?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We'll see if we can head him off at the printer my Lord. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Subject to observations from your Lordship, or any direction as I proceed, I'm going to follow the submission as we have set it out, but seek to do so with brevity where I can, there are some points that I need to elaborate and enlarge upon, and also at appropriate points to deal with the principal matters raised by the prosecution.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. That would be helpful. As you would expect, I've read both sets of submissions. I obviously haven't delved into the authorities in detail. You can refer me to anything as you see fit and as you wish, but take it that I have the basic respective submissions.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm grateful, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We make the submission primarily in the case of four counts where air embolus is alleged to be the sole cause of death or collapse. Those are counts 1 -- I set these out now so all can follow the purpose of the submission: Count 1, the case of [Baby A], which is an allegation of murder.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Count 2, which is [Baby B], an allegation of attempted murder.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Count 4, [Baby D], allegation of murder.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And count 16, [Baby M], an allegation of attempted murder.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Air embolus is alleged to be the sole cause of death in those counts.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We have then set out in paragraph 2 those counts in which air embolus is a cause of death or collapse. They are as follows: In count 3 [Baby C], which is an allegation of murder, and in that count Dr Dewi Evans has alleged air embolus and also air via the NGT, the nasogastric tube.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Count 5, the case of [Baby E], an allegation of murder. Dewi Evans has also alleged trauma in addition to air embolus.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Count 12, the case of [Baby I], which is an allegation of murder. There are a number of events there and the events on 13 October, the 14th and the night of the 22nd and 23rd all, to one extent or another, involve an allegation of air embolus, although not the sole allegation.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Count 17, which is the first count dealing with [Baby N], attempted murder. Air embolus has been alleged by Dewi Evans.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Finally, in count 20, [Baby O], murder. Air embolus is the mechanism alleged, although there are other mechanisms alleged to contribute or be responsible, and those have been set out in the argument.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Our submission is that medical evidence is fundamental to these allegations. I'm going to return to that shortly, but we submit that the scientific basis for air embolus is so weak that it fails to provide the level of reliability required to support these allegations. And for that reason, we submit that a jury, properly directed, could not properly convict on it.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We have set out the relevant part of the R v Galbraith and the element that applies is what's sometimes called the second limb of Galbraith, we maintain, which is that the evidence is inherently so weak or vague, or in this case we say inherently so unreliable on a scientific basis, that it cannot properly support the allegations that are made, which are central to these allegations. That is why we say on counts 1, 2, 4 and 16 there is no case to answer. And in counts 3, 5, 12, 17 and 20, we respectfully submit that, insofar as this evidence has been relied upon to support a conviction, the jury should be directed to disregard it.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Before I go further with the body of our submission, I'll deal now with a number of points raised by the prosecution to assist the court and I make apology if in doing so I haven't digested the full import of any aspect of them. I will wait to hear if it's different from how I see it.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Exactly, yes. This is in anticipation, so it's your understanding, so obviously you'll have a right of response.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm grateful. There are three matters that I am going to deal with at this stage, which run through the prosecution response. The first is the propriety of the submission of no case to answer at this point and what's said about that; the prosecution say it is an abuse.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The second is whether the medical evidence alone is enough to base this submission upon given the circumstantial evidence that the prosecution identify the fact there are other counts, there are other matters to take into account, and therefore even if there is merit or any weight to the defence submissions, they do not dispose of those counts. Problems with the medical evidence, in other words, is not fatal to the count insofar as there are any problems recognised, and they would dispute that there are problems. We recognise that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The final point that I'll deal with at this stage, and I come to it, is the position of Dr Hall, who has featured in the prosecution response as a reason to support their position in resisting the defence application. I'll go through them in that order because that's really the way they come through in the prosecution argument.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: First of all, the question of the defence making a submission of no case to answer and the criticisms by the prosecution, in particular, are at paragraphs 7 and 8 of their argument. They culminate in the proposition that in effect this is an abuse of the process by the defence; that appears at paragraph 25.1. That's their first ground of resistance to this application.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We don't accept any of that for a moment. The purpose of this application, absolutely plainly, from its terms and its content is the sufficiency of medical evidence, in particular whether or not the basis for what might be called a theory of air embolus is sufficiently well-established and reliable to support the allegations where they are made in the different counts. That's the purpose of this and our submission is it falls, when looked at collectively, a long way from the level of strength and reliability that scientific evidence should have in a case like this.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That submission is based entirely on the evidence as it has unfolded during this trial.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I could not possibly have stood here at the start of this trial and turned to 500 pages of evidence, or parts of those pages, in support of the submissions that we make on behalf of the defence if this trial had not taken place and we had not got to this stage. The basis for this application is the state of the prosecution evidence at the end of their case.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We submit that it is extraordinary -- this isn't intended to be rude -- but badly judged to criticise the defence for an entirely proper application that they are entitled to make as a part of the trial process at the conclusion of the prosecution case, and we respectfully submit, on the basis of the way the prosecution evidence on air embolus has unfolded, it cannot
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: possibly be a matter of surprise that there is heavy criticism of that. That may not have been possible at the outset but most definitely is, we submit, well-grounded now. And we are compelled to observe that it simply isn't right to talk about abuse when the defence make use of the proper entitlement to critique the evidence on the basis of how it has unfolded.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: If it is the view that even at the outset this evidence would not have been admissible, that could only add weight to the application that we make. But this isn't about admissibility at this point. We have made it very plain: this is about weight, the court having now heard this evidence. And our submission is the evidence of air embolus is inherently so weak and inconsistent that it cannot support a conviction.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That takes me to the second broad point as we perceive it, raised by the prosecution, which is that criticisms or shortcomings, if there be any, in the medical evidence alone are insufficient to meet what's required in this submission and the test the defence must satisfy.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: In particular, your Lordship will find reference to that, and the way the prosecution deal with it, in paragraphs 21 to 23 of their response, which look at the interplay, although very briefly, but we understand why of course, between different counts on this indictment -- that's a matter that will have to be considered at some point if not now, but at some point -other evidence, circumstantial evidence, and other factors by which they say Lucy Letby is implicated in these deaths.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So I deal now with that, that whatever the state of the medical evidence, that isn't enough for the defence to bring this argument. We submit that isn't right, respectfully submit that isn't right in the particular circumstances of these allegations.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: In making that submission, my Lord, we start with the authority of Holdsworth, which the prosecution dwell upon in their response and go through the facts to show how they are different from this case, and of course they are different form this case. Serious as they are, they are certainly not on the scale we're dealing with here. I don't mean on the individual case but in terms of the number of counts looked at in the evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Holdsworth [2008] EWCA Crim 971, at paragraph 12 of our argument.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We cite it because in that paragraph the Court of Appeal made very clear the high requirement, we submit, of medical evidence. What was said was this:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "Conclusions of medical experts on the cause of an injury or death necessarily involve a process of deduction, that is inferring conclusion from given facts based on other knowledge and experience. But particular caution is needed where the scientific knowledge of the process or processes involved is or may be incomplete. As knowledge increases today's orthodoxy may become tomorrow's outdated learning. Special caution is also needed where expert evidence is not just relied upon as additional material to support a prosecution but is fundamental to it."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That's the starting point of what we say about the law and the high requirement for reliability with scientific evidence. That isn't where we end and I'll return to where we go with that in due course. But this relates to what the prosecution say in two ways.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: First of all, that where there is medical evidence, as the court said in Holdsworth, there is special caution to be exercised in the way that it is approached. We don't go on from that to suggest there's any particular complexity in that concept. The courts are well-used to those areas where particular caution is urged in other parts of the law. But it's important that it says that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Secondly:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "That is particularly so where the evidence is fundamental to the allegation."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The prosecution in this response have gone into other details and circumstantial evidence and we understand that. But the medical evidence, we submit, is front and centre with these allegations and that is why we spent most of the last 6 months dealing with it in, at times, minute detail in this trial, with a succession of experts that would be hard to parallel, I suspect, in any other case.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: If a mechanism is alleged in this case and the evidence is not sufficiently strong to support that, we submit that is a fundamental problem. A reason for that is that in this case, causation and the issues relating to that are firmly rooted in medical explanations. For example, this isn't -- I don't put this as a lurid explanation, but in a case, for example, of a gangland murder, an example may be given of a missing body case. The idea that there might be some medical cause or any medical basis for what's taken place as an explanation for the missing body or what happened is implausible unless, for example, there's a good basis for that. In those cases, a case like that and many other cases, of course circumstantial evidence may
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: weigh the more heavily and it may be the only evidence available.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: But in this case we're dealing with a hospital setting, babies, many of whom are unwell or very fragile physically, as a starting point and certainly at risk of deterioration so far as their condition is concerned.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Therefore it isn't a case where it can easily be assumed that there must be deliberate harm in the absence of the prosecution being able to establish what harm there was.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That assumption cannot apply.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: In medical cases, we submit, and this is why we have put the two authorities that we do before the court, and I'll go to it shortly, in cases that might be described as having a preeminently medical causation, a cause may not be identified, but in no way does it follow that culpable harm should therefore be inferred.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Of course that's a question of degree, we recognise that. Sometimes the extent of circumstantial evidence may be so great that it still calls for an explanation.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It may well be that is where the prosecution end up, if I can put it that way, with this application. We submit that is a significant shift in the case we've been dealing with up to this point where the mechanisms have been crucial because in the absence of them it's simply unascertained and may in fact be a medical cause unidentified, however many times that happens. It could be the same cause unidentified. It has been crucial to this prosecution to advance explanations because of the circumstances and they have sought to do so and most definitely presented the case in that way.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We listened closely to the opening, as your Lordship did, and again the predominance lay on the medical evidence and what it went to prove and that is what a large part of this trial has dealt with.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The authorities we sent through, once we had received the prosecution application, Cannings and Henderson, are authorities we anticipate the court will be familiar with, although there's obviously some detail in them. Both of them involve infant death in circumstances of alleged homicide.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: In the case of Cannings a multiple death, although again, I observe, not to the scale we deal with in this case. And, in the case of Henderson, what's called -- I apologise for any
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: inelegance -- a baby-shaking case; that's how it's described by the Court of Appeal.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The reason that we cite those two authorities is they support what we say about the dangers of working on the basis that if the prosecution haven't identified a mechanism one can therefore infer deliberate harm.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: In Cannings we take your Lordship to paragraph 13.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Just give me a moment because I was only alerted to this, as you'll appreciate, minutes before the hearing started. I'm not being critical. I've been dealing with other things as well.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (Pause)
So we're looking first of all at Cannings?
Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I'm getting that up now. I have it.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's the proposition or, rather, the statement of the court at paragraph 13 we go to. The court was dealing with what inferences can be drawn in what's called a sudden infant death case in terms of the explanations that are provided and the alternatives in the absence of full explanation.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We start at the second sentence, the first sentence follows on from that discussion, but it's where the court says this:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "Whether there are one, two or even three deaths the exclusion of currently known natural causes of infant death does not establish that the death or deaths resulted from the deliberate infliction of harm. That represents not only the legal principle which must be applied in any event, but in addition we shall see at the very least it appears to us to coincide with the views of a reputable body of expert medical opinion."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We don't go into the expert medical opinion in that case, it's the legal principle that we rely upon.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We submit that in the case of Henderson, some years later, which is at 2010, England and Wales Court of Appeal, Crim 1269, that principle or its sense is found and restated by the court at paragraph 44. We'll also go to 78. But at paragraph 44 the court said:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "We must recognise the limits of medical science and in particular that there may be events, deaths or symptoms which
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: are unexplained and unforeseen. Further, any conclusion must acknowledge the importance of the burden of proof in the context of cases such as these."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Cases such as these are cases turning on medical expert evidence:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "It is not for the defence to provide any explanation. The mere fact that it is unable to do so is not of itself a sound basis for concluding that the prosecution's evidence is correct."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We submit that is not the same words as in paragraph 13 of Cannings, but it approaches the matter -- the same matter in a different way. And I look next, my Lord, and take your Lordship to paragraph 78, which is a statement really specific to the case but it touches again on the principle:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "Further it is important to note that [this is the trial judge] stressed the defence was under no obligation to advance any particular theory as to cause of death and the rejection of the theory of spontaneous seizure did not of itself mean that the jury was required to accept the prosecution case and convict."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Of course, there we recognise that's the court identifying how a jury can be directed to deal with cases where medical evidence is textured in a way that there are decisions to be taken as to its strength or where alternative causes have to be considered.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: But we submit that looking at the authorities, and I've only gone to them briefly, but simply to support the proposition I advance to your Lordship, that in a case with medical evidence, there may be an unidentified cause and that if the case proceeds on the basis that although the prosecution haven't identified a cause, nevertheless in some way that remains an issue, and that doesn't dispose of the prosecution case. The danger is that the burden then falls on the defence to meet that in some way.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: In fact, to assist, it seems to me there are two propositions there. The first -- this seems to be where we get to with the argument I advance in light of this response, the first is that the prosecution evidence on cause is fundamental in this case and the way this case has been presented.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: If it is not of sufficient strength to be reliable in the way scientific evidence should be then the counts that rely upon it, or those parts of the counts that rely upon it, are fatally undermined when the test of Galbraith is applied.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The second proposition in meeting this response from the prosecution, relying upon the principles identified, we submit, from the Court of Appeal, are that there is a danger in medical
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: cases of, in effect, reversing the burden where the prosecution have sought to advance, as they have here, medical evidence, which in fact cannot go to establish cause properly in the way the prosecution seek to establish but, we submit, if the case then proceeds, with the defendant in effect called upon to explain what has happened when there may be an unidentified medical cause.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That's why we submit it's particularly important for the court to keep in mind the setting of these allegations as against the generality of cases where it may be more easily said by the prosecution, well, there's a lot of circumstantial evidence here, what on earth is this unidentified cause? A perfectly healthy person has gone missing, we don't know what's happened, there's no medical issues to look at in particular, in the absence of any explanation, there's a very good basis for considering some sort of guilt or harm.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That doesn't follow in this case, we submit, and so for that reason seeking to meet the defence submission by pointing to other bits of evidence elsewhere neither reflects the way in which this prosecution case is advanced nor in fact, we respectfully observe, the way the evidence should be analysed at this point. So that's what we say with regard to the prosecution submission that there is evidence outwith the medical evidence that can compensate for any deficiencies.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Just so I understand this, you are therefore saying that because of the nature of the evidence in relation to air embolus, no consideration should be attached to any other evidence because the cause of death cannot confidently be relied upon, the asserted cause of death cannot be relied upon, therefore the court should not look at any other evidence just to indicate, to assist in relation to a potential natural or unnatural causes of death? Is that what you're saying?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The order in which that's dealt with is significant. We submit that if the medical evidence does not establish cause as alleged (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: If the medical evidence has to establish cause of death and if it doesn't then one doesn't look at any other evidence, we just disregard any other evidence?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: On that count, yes. Most particularly, when dealing with the air embolus counts, that ends them entirely. There are other causes alleged or other possibilities on the other counts, the other five counts --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Oh, I understand that.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: But on those particular four counts, yes, our submission is that this case has been powerfully based upon the allegation that this is an air embolus. The prosecution, in effect, are saying: we have the answer, we can say what this is, and upon that basis we submit that's what it is. Because in the absence of that, we submit, the evidence is not strong enough to support what's alleged. There may be various circumstantial matters but they're not decisive and they're not strong enough. It's the air embolus evidence that is pivotal and has been throughout.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I understand that is the submission.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That's the way we've put that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Can I then at this point raise a question I will ask: is it in dispute that air embolus can cause death?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We haven't suggested it cannot cause death. As a fact, air embolus is capable of causing death. But we observe, without any sense of glibness whatsoever, that so are very many things, and seeking to tie the case to air embolus is a very specific mechanism. And the fact of death is in no way probative, we submit, of air embolus, and indeed that's one of the issues and one of our criticisms, that there's been great inconsistency on that point.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I understand that.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: But as a possible mechanism, yes, of course it's recognised, if it's proved sufficiently, then of course it can be a mechanism of death, yes. We haven't taken issue with that and we don't.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Okay. Sorry, I interrupted you. Please carry on. I just wanted to be clear in particular about what you were saying about the air embolus counts and where it's either the sole -- said to be the sole cause of death or a cause of death.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes. Well, it's well-established and recognised, air embolism in principle can cause death. The question is whether the -- this argument at this stage of the case is whether the expert evidence on which that mechanism has been supposedly identified and applied -- the submission is it's so poor, it's inherently unreliable, that it doesn't support that finding.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It would be like saying, of course, that a bullet can cause death but the expert evidence on ballistics is so poor you can never actually prove that's what's happened.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Crucially also, I should say this, my Lord, part of that, twinned with that is the fact that it isn't accepted that air embolus is identified in these cases.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: As a mechanism it can cause death, but there's certainly no concession that that is what's happened or what accounts for any piece of evidence in this case. That's tied up with the application that we make because we submit that where the expert evidence has sought to identify characteristics from which air embolus can be diagnosed, if it can be, they are fundamentally flawed as well.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So as a matter of principle, of course it can cause death, but we submit that's as far as that gets on this evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Right, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Can I deal next with the third matter, third principal matter we submit the prosecution raise, which is the position of Dr Hall. We submit that for the purpose of this submission, that is entirely irrelevant.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It is not evidence in the case, it is not before the jury, it hasn't featured in the trial. It may never feature in the trial. That doesn't indicate what's going to happen with Dr Hall, but it may or may not.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The court will appreciate that it has to consider the evidence as it's presented to the court now at the close of the prosecution case.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: His evidence plays no part in this application. The criticisms that Dr Hall has made of air embolus in this case, the criticisms that he's made of prosecution experts alleging air embolus are not matters we have sought to rely upon and we can no more seek to rely upon them to support our argument than, curiously, the prosecution regard Dr Hall as an expert on air embolus and seek to rely on it on their behalf. It is, respectfully, misconceived to try to use a defence expert who hasn't been called to meet a criticism of the prosecution evidence at this part of the case and it is a surprising recourse to take, and surprising because it's not in evidence and a basic feature of a submission of no case to answer is it looks at the evidence before the jury.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It's surprising because, so far as we understand, and the court may have perceived, the prosecution in general do not accept either large parts of what Dr Hall says or his conclusions. And it's particularly surprising because the prosecution vigorously resisted the introduction of Dr Hall's evidence during their case, absolutely resisted it, and sought a ruling from your
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Lordship to that effect. It ill behoves them now, having in fact sought to prevent it from featuring in the case at this point, and it not featuring, to then seek to gain what they perceive to be some benefit by a reference to it when dealing with a defence application.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So we submit it plays no part in this, it could play no part in it, and it should play in part in it.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We also add this, just in parentheses, keeping in mind the criticisms made about the objective of the defence application. We applied for Dr Hall to give evidence at the start of this case. Your Lordship will have seen the criticism that somehow this was all mapped out by the defence when we began this application. In fact, even if it was, that wouldn't matter. But as it happens, it was the defence who sought Dr Hall to give evidence so the matter could be contested in detail as we proceeded, believing there would be a contest on the evidence, and there most certainly has been, but without Dr Hall participating in it.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: But that observation takes me back to the first part of the response to the prosecution response, which is that this is an entirely proper application to make on the basis of the evidence at this part of the case, but Dr Hall can play no part in that we submit respectfully.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: My Lord, those are the principal responses to the prosecution response. Of course, underlying their response in general is the argument, and I don't seek to be able to do justice to what Mr Johnson would say, but we perceive the argument that in any event any weakness is just a matter of the type of weakness a jury can deal with in the course of a case and be directed to do so appropriately and therefore what the defence complain of doesn't amount to what their submission relies upon.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So perhaps keeping that basic response to the defence in mind, and that basic exercise that I respectfully submit your Lordship will conduct in weighing up what is the way to deal with any perceived deficiencies in the evidence, perhaps I can then return to the main body of the submission.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Certainly.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Not all of it, that's unnecessary, but just to illustrate some of the points that we make and why it is that we say this evidence is just fundamentally unreliable. The authority of Dlugosz, 2013, England and Wales Court of Appeal, Criminal 2, our paragraph 13, states what is now in fact incorporated in the Criminal Practice Directions, which is that
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: it is essential to recall the principle, which is applicable, namely in determining the issue -- this was of admissibility:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "The court must be satisfied that there is sufficiently reliable scientific basis for the evidence to be admitted."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The Criminal Practice Direction at paragraphs A.4, A.5 and 19A.6, which is in the defence bundle, pages 1 to 4, sets out the approach to that, and of course Dlugosz, which was a case turning on low copy DNA, was looking at the admissibility of evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: As we submitted, we are not arguing admissibility here, but we submit that the type of factors identified in the Criminal Practice Direction in particular at paragraph 19A.5, are the type of factors to bear in mind when the court comes to consider the strength or reliability of scientific evidence in this case. They are set out at (a) through to (h). Although I may make some reference to specific ones as we go ahead it's probably unnecessary for me to read out everything it says there, but it is questions like the extent of the data on which an expert relies, that's at 19A.5(a), how inferences are made, how results are relied upon, input by others and peer review, that's at 19A.5(d), questions of evidence falling outside the expert's sphere of expertise, which we submit looms large in fact when looking at the prosecution experts, and completeness of information available to the expert, the consideration of a range of expert opinion, that's at (f) and (g).
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We note also, significantly, at paragraph 19A.6, potential flaws, as they're described in the Criminal Practice Direction, flaws that may mean that the opinion is less reliable. For example, 19A.6(a):
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "Being based on a hypothesis which has not been subjected to sufficient scrutiny including, where appropriate, experimental or other testing or which has failed to stand up to scrutiny."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We pick that one out in particular because on a number of occasions when questioned, prosecution experts, certainly in the cases of Dr Evans, consultant paediatric, Dr Bohin, consultant neonatologist, and Professor Arthurs, consultant paediatric radiologist, have all at certain points said, "We just don't have the studies or the data to answer that question". For example, how long it would take for how much air to have a particular effect. And we have identified examples where experiments have been made on adults, data from adults, experiments from dogs or rabbits, that type of response. I will go to one as an illustration in due course.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We submit that while there may be some academic sympathy with an expert trying to grapple with a question for which there is insufficient data because those experiments cannot be conducted, that is a problem in the halls of scholarship. But when we are in the environment we are in now, the implications of that change and we are, of course, dealing with questions of what can be proved. And the fact there may be inabilities to conduct experiments which would give the answer should not be an answer to an insufficiency of data or empirical evidence. And the flaw described in 19A.6(a), we submit, chimes precisely with that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I will turn to the experts very briefly -- very shortly, sorry — and deal with them, knowing your Lordship will have looked at the detail here and has, of course, listened to this evidence during the course of the trial. We know that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: There's one passage in a way which, we say, absolutely encapsulates -- there's a number of passages but there's one I'm going to go to now which encapsulates the problem with air embolus in this case.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I will take your Lordship there. It comes from the evidence, in fact, of Dr Sandie Bohin, the prosecution neonatologist. It's at page 410 of the bundle. I'll give your Lordship time to get there of course.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It's evidence that she gave in the case of [Baby N], count 17 on the indictment. It's at page 410.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I have 410. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's also -- this is referred to in the Sandie Bohin section of our submission at paragraph 47 as an example of where finally we get to with Dr Bohin and what we say is the unacceptable levels in the variation of skin discolouration that she maintained could assist in identifying air embolus.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: At this point, and it's at internal page numbering 155 through to 156, and she was asked the question at line 16 at 155:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "Question: Across the whole of this trial, we don't have a constant by which we can measure air embolus, do we?"
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I should say this was in the context of description of discolouration. Your Lordship will see that. In fact, it will help just to look at line 13, just above that, I asked Dr Bohin:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "Question: So far, we don't have any constant description of any discolouration, do we?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "Answer: Not in this case."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Pausing there, we've identified in these submissions how actually the starting point in this case was that there was a specific discolouration advanced, most clearly by all the experts who gave evidence upon this, which is that description in the Lee and Tanswell paper, and I'll return to that. But that was the starting point. In fact various discolourations were then used as evidence of air embolus, which led to this, towards the end of this issue being explored in evidence:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "Question: We don't have a constant description of any discolouration, do we?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "Answer: Not in this case.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "Question: Across the whole of this trial we don't have a constant by which we can measure air embolus do, we?"
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "Answer: I think what's come out across the whole of this trial is a huge variation on the types of skin changes seen by the parents, practitioners, nursing practitioners and doctors of these children. And certainly the medical and nursing personnel are very clear they've not seen changes like this before or since but that the changes appear quite graphic. So although there's not one single thing you can say is definitely pathognomonic of air embolus, that's a bit like saying all chickenpox rashes are different [as read]."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And we then went to chickenpox. But it's --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "All chickenpox rashes are not" --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "... are not different."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: But it's what she said at the beginning of that answer that we say captures the problem:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "Answer: I think what's come out across the whole of this trial is a huge variation on the types of skin changes seen by parents, practitioners..."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And so on. That sounds very much like the trial process being used as a learning process and a source of data, what's come out in the course of the trial is...
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That is a clear example of constructing a theory in the light of evidence that's come out. That is ex post facto theorising, utterly self-serving. I don't say that to be rude to Dr Bohin but that's what's happening.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And it's fundamentally wrong because, first of all, that is based upon a presumption before the analysis had been applied that we are dealing with air embolus. What she's actually saying there is: well, these are all cases of air embolus, I know I began by saying in Lee and Tanswell that's the description, or agreeing that's the description we have, and that was most relevant at the start of the case with [Baby A] and [Baby B], but in effect what's happening is she is saying, well, now that we have seen all these cases of air embolus we now know it presents with very varied discolourations.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So first of all, it indicates a presumption that we're dealing with air embolus and then seeking to justify that and, secondly, it shows just how unreliable this aspect, for example, of the expert evidence is because in effect she is ex post facto constructing the air embolus theory at the end of the case, having, we observe, been asked at the beginning as to the factors that define air embolus, asked in cross-examination, it wasn't set out before then, but asked in cross-examination, and discolouration in keeping with that identified in Lee and Tanswell was the starting point.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: By the end of it, this expert is saying:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "Answer: I think that what's come out across the whole of this trial is a huge variation in the types of skin discolourations."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Well, that sounds, as we say, that the trial has almost been used as a source of self-serving evidence to prove what air embolus is because it has come out: actually, look at all these air emboli and what different colours they all have. We submit that's one illustration but one that gets to the nub of the shortcomings of this evidence and why it is so unreliable.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The position of the experts is dealt with by Dewi Evans at paragraph 19, as I've indicated. Knowing your Lordship will have been through this material and listened to the case, it's unnecessary for me to set out everything that's here. In short, like the other experts in this case, he has no clinical experience of diagnosing air embolus. He simply doesn't.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: One thing is that air embolus is rare.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: All the experts have said air embolus is rare.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So it may be very difficult to find anyone who has direct experience and knowledge of air embolus, which is unquestionably air embolus. Now, does that mean that therefore one cannot rely on any of the circumstances in relation to the
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: collapses of the babies which an expert says is consistent with an air embolus?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It cannot be relied on.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Can I just clarify, does your Lordship mean by circumstances the medical circumstances around it or the --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Just generally. This is one of the difficulties. All we essentially have in relation to observable changes to someone who is suffering an air embolus in life is this description from the Lee and Tanswell paper. This paper cites no more than five or six cases out of 50 where discolouration was present.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So the starting point there is that it is about 10% of the cases where there was any discolouration. Right?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Of these, only one instance described the presentation that was regarded as the defining discolouration of air embolus at the outset of this case, this is you, and that description was:
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "Blanching and migrating areas of cutaneous pallor were noted in several cases and in one of our own cases we noted bright pink vessels against a generally cyanosed cutaneous background."
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So that is the extent of the evidence in relation to discolouration.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, it is, my Lord, and that is why we submit it is more crucial, not less crucial, for it to be construed restrictively in how it's applied because where there's uncertainty in medical or scientific knowledge, or where it's at the boundaries of a particular area, and perhaps uncertainty is the better way of putting it here, it's important to be, we respectfully submit, more careful with the interpretation and application of what learning there is than to say, well, this is very difficult, so there's going to be a degree of latitude that might not otherwise be acceptable. I'm not suggesting that follows from what your Lordship says, but there's a danger that lack of specificity justifies vagueness or imprecision from that point on.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We submit that where a mechanism or a scientific theory is applied in a criminal trial, it has to be sufficiently reliable. If there is limited data available and limited experience then, insofar as there are characteristics that can be identified, at the very least they should be applied rigorously.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Our submission, a large part of our submission is based not just on the fact that the starting point is not strong, we say, not strong because none of these clinicians actually have personal experience, and we say not strong because there is actually very little research and available data. But an important part of the criticisms we make is that, that having been acknowledged, from that point onwards in notable circumstances there have been constant variations to meet the exigencies of the evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And where we get to with Dr Bohin and [Baby N], where ex post facto she incorporates a degree of variation into how air embolus can manifest itself based on her experience in looking at a trial in cases that she is treating as air embolus before it's been established on the basis of discolouration, that goes to show the dangers of that approach.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So with the authorities, Henderson, which talks about:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "Today's orthodoxy gets replaced by tomorrow's new learning."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And other cases looking at what is at the boundaries of knowledge, it is crucial to at least be -- for experts to be principled in their application of it.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I don't mean anything disreputable: by principled I mean stick with the principles we have.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Our submission is that the principles in the first place are weak and the experience is weak. But even if that were to be regarded as an unavoidable inevitability in the trial, and we say respectfully it shouldn't be, even if it were, the way that they have then been applied afterwards, in particular by Dr Evans and Dr Bohin, goes way beyond the acceptable limits of what can be done with that starting material and has become strikingly inconsistent or variable or unreliable.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And so unreliable, you say, and inconsistent, that there is not a basis in respect of the counts in question — let's just look at the ones where it is said to be the sole cause -- not a basis upon which a jury could be invited to conclude that there is sufficient evidence in the case as a whole to found a conviction?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, we do submit that because the scientific theory is unreliable --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I understand that.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: -- and that's the test.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's it.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: With regard to evidence that can exist for air embolus, may I just take your Lordship, following through from the enquiry your Lordship raised, to page 509 of the defence bundle, which is the section of the Lee and Tanswell article that we've seen on a number of occasions, but it isn't the descriptions of colour that I take your Lordship to.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The bottom right corner, 508 on the top left, but the bundle numbering is 509. As your Lordship has --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Well, I just quoted what you put in your written submission.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Exactly. It comes from that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That's the passage from which it comes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It is. But following on from that, we submit it's significant that there are sources of evidence that can far more directly diagnose air embolus, none of which feature in this case. I'm just going to identify this for your Lordship because it isn't as perhaps as in the dark as might otherwise appear from what the experts have said in this case, all of whom put significant store on this article.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Reading on, in fact, from the section that your Lordship has just referred to, a couple of lines down we have:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "The most distinctive sign of pulmonary vascular air embolism..."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I just confirm -- does your Lordship...?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I'm on page 509.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: About three or four lines below the passage your Lordship referred to. It's the first paragraph, the lengthy paragraph under the table. If your Lordship just tracks that down about five or six lines, you'll come to the description of colour and then three or four lines below that, halfway across the line it begins:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "The most distinctive sign of pulmonary vascular air embolism observed in half of the reported cases is a finding of free air when blood is withdrawn from the umbilical arterial catheter. Columns of air or a frothy mixture of blood and air were often obtained."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: In fact what this article does is identify phenomena which do, it seems, directly indicate air embolus, none of which are found in this case. It may be that the circumstances mean they were not found because they couldn't be because these tests weren't conducted, but it wouldn't be right to say there is no way of accurately identifying air embolus.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: They go on to say:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "Another related phenomenon observed in two reported patients and in one of our infants was an inappropriately high arterial oxygen concentration recorded from intra-aortic oxygen electrodes in direct contact with gas bubbles."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Then, and this is something that was raised with some witnesses:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "A radiograph is diagnostic and free air may be seen in both the arterial and venous systems as well as in the heart."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And then it refers to the figure at the top of the page, which in fact Professor Arthurs was taken to by me at one point in his evidence in slightly clearer image.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It goes on to say on this topic:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "In 75% of reported cases the radiographs were taken antemortem."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Which is an issue that's occupied this court in fact:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "Post-mortem radiographs..."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Pausing there, my Lord, in 75% of reported cases of air embolus, the radiographs were taken ante-mortem. So it would appear it's capable of being diagnostic, depending on the circumstances. Then:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "Post-mortem radiographs need to be interpreted with caution as intravascular air may appear as early as 25 minutes after death."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Of course that has some bearing on what Professor Arthurs has said, but that's not the reason I go to that now. I go to that because there is more direct evidence available in particular circumstances of air embolus.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Now, it may be, for one reason or another, these sources of evidence are simply not available in the cases we're dealing with here. But if that's right, then of course, we respectfully observe, it doesn't follow that the next best alternative is what we have to work with because the next best alternative may
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: not have sufficient reliability to support the allegation that's made and that is the test. No matter what justifications are given for a paucity of research or experience, that's the test.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: My Lord, I'm going to move to the section that deals with Sally Kinsey and then Owen Arthurs. That is not because we don't set significant store by our criticisms of Dr Evans and Dr Bohin.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: No, but there's nothing you wish to add to what's in writing?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No, nothing I wish to add. That just simply elaborates on what your Lordship has.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Professor Kinsey, who was a retired paediatric haematologist, was called to give evidence in particular on the question of discolouration. And we've either cited or included within the argument key factors relating to her evidence that, we submit, mean -- in fact, as she accepted -- that she is no expert on this topic. In fact, that line of questioning concluded -- and we've included in our paragraph 53 -- which was she ended up saying:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "I was asked if I could make a bit more of an explanation about the features of an air embolus. I did say at the time I was not an expert in this area but I was asked if I could do it anyway."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: She dealt with how discolouration could happen because of air embolus, referring to Lee and Tanswell and also a paper by the writers Garcia and Mitchell. In fact, that's a paper she cited, a key paper she cited in her statement of 1 November 2022.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: But as she accepted, my Lord, that statement dealt with deep sea divers, adults, overweight, as it happens, and comes from a journal called Diving and Hyperbaric Medicine, which establishes:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "Medical treatment in which an ambient pressure greater than sea level atmospheric pressure is a necessary component."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And it is classically what divers have when they come from depths, the decompression sickness that they have.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The bends.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, the bends. She accepted -- we have put the references here -- that that isn't of general application, it's a very limited area, and rather like what Dr Bohin had to say about dogs and rabbits and adults, but the more so, certainly so
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: far as adults are concerned, there is no proper basis for taking that and applying it to neonates in the circumstances of this case, and she didn't suggest there was.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: She, rather like the comment that we identify from Dr Bohin -her evidence on this, in general, is, we respectfully submit, an object lesson of the potential pitfalls here because she's somebody who's a professor of haematology and on the basis that she works with blood and circulation, she was prevailed upon to assist, in effect, to help out with how discolouration could occur with air embolus and in due course be used as diagnostic in this case. And as she accepted, what she had to say about the circulation and gas exchange was of general application, she is no specialist in this, and the material she relies on to talk about discolouration is outside her field of expert and is highly limited, the Lee and Tanswell and then the Garcia report, which is really about something entirely different.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Owen Arthurs, my Lord, Professor Arthurs, is a paediatric radiologist, working at Great Ormond Street. There was, when he first gave evidence, cross-examination of the process he went through to reach the conclusion that gas in a great vessel or vessels post-mortem is unusual. Cross-examination was designed to look at that process critically.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It is helpful, we submit, to keep in mind the factors, in particular at paragraph 19A.5 of that Criminal Practice Direction, when considering what Dr Arthurs said. There's no doubting the diligence with which he went about his study. The paragraph I should say, 19A.5 of the practice direction, is found at pages 1 and 2 of the defence bundle.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And set out in paragraph 14 of your --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And you've gone through it.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We have. In many ways, again, illustrations of the problems presented by this evidence emerge with Professor Arthurs. For example, a process which he has conducted, there is no peer review of this, it's one study he conducted with the available material of children, of a relatively limited population, in fact, babies as close as he could find them to those in this case, neonates at Great Ormond Street. We don't doubt his intention to produce research that was as strong as he could make it. But the group that he could draw upon is necessarily, we would submit, limited.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: In terms of evidence-based medicine, he agreed it wasn't of the highest order and we submit it's certainly not of the highest
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: and it would certainly struggle to pass muster in an academic journal, not least because, we submit, there aren't the necessary or controls that would be in place in terms of criteria to be applied at the outset, how things are going to be measured against that peer review, which is important. The size of the sample group, which is very small, to be used as general application in this case.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And of course, against that, in fairness to Professor Arthurs, is the fact that he identified other mechanisms or other causes that could account for the air that was seen in the great vessel or vessels in this case.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So even with a process that, we submit, would fall short of the criteria or the type of criteria in paragraph 19A.5, even at the end of that and interpreting it as generously as possible, it certainly doesn't go to identify air embolus with specificity. We still end up with a 25% chance that it is post-mortem gas of some sort, though he said that's usually where there has been trauma of some sort.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: But one bears in mind what's also in this case, the Lee and Tanswell article, which talks about post-mortem has more generally appearing within some minutes, in fact, of death. He also identified other explanations which may be applicable in this case, so we submit that it was a purpose-built study by him for a trial in which he was a witness, about which he came to give evidence about his own study at his own hospital with subjects that he chose that hasn't been peer-reviewed.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That isn't to criticise his intentions, but it's to criticise the method.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Finally my Lord, so far as experts are concerned, Andreas Marnerides, who is a paediatric pathologist and histopathologist, did not in fact, we submit, contribute to the issue that is under consideration here, which is whether or not there is a sufficiently reliable body of expert evidence to apply when air embolus is under consideration. And in fact, when cross-examined about the mechanism of air embolus in a neonate and how it operates, and this is in our paragraph 69, he was either unable or, we have to say, unwilling to explain it because he kept on saying, "I'm not a clinician, I deal with the point of death, I can't explain how this happens", and he wouldn't.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We understand the limits around a professional expert witness and what they can give evidence upon, but we submit that were it to be said that he is an expert on the general sphere of air embolus, it's a very poor starting point that he felt unable to describe how it works in a neonate and he didn't really set
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: himself out as that. His role was principally to see whether there were alternative causes from the pathology that could account, in individual cases, for death and also whether there were any findings that in an individual case might be capable of supporting air embolus. And the only one of those, in fact, was in the case of [Baby A] when he described microscopic bubbles in slides, some of which had come from the lungs and some of which had come from the brain.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: All credit to him, he didn't seek to say that's diagnostic or conclusive, but in light of what the clinicians or the radiology would show, it's something that could be supportive of it. But we have no description of how an air embolus comes to do that or how it would fit in with it. He has identified air, possibly and how that may play a part in one of the charges on this indictment, but he cannot deal with the question of the reliability of the evidence in terms of establishing a theory that can be applied. And given his reliance upon the clinicians, which he was very clear about, however we approach Dr Marnerides, and he only really bites on that one count in this respect, however we approach it he cannot get beyond the quality of the expert evidence on air embolus insofar as it comes from Drs Bohin, Evans and Professor Arthurs. He relies very heavily on what they say and proposes no alternative.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: My Lord, those are the principal contentions that we raise with the submission that we make.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: In conclusion, we submit that this evidence is fundamental to counts 1, 2, 4 and 16, and on the evidence it is insufficiently reliable when measured against what is required of scientific evidence and when measured against its prominence and significance in this case up to now. It is insufficiently reliable to support conviction on those four counts and, for the same reasons we submit, insofar as it has been used to support the allegation on counts 3, 5, 12, 17 and 20, it should form part of that medical evidence no longer, howsoever that is achieved, which is a different question, but that's where we get to.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: If we can assist now, my Lord, we will, otherwise we'll assist after your Lordship's heard the prosecution.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: You will have the right of reply after Mr Johnson has addressed me.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Mr Johnson, thank you for your written response. I appreciate the constraints of time obviously have an impact.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: You should feel free to add or emphasise anything that you wish.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Submissions by MR JOHNSON
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you. Can I start with one of the fundamental principles of an English criminal trial.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's the burden of proof and it's a point that my learned friend raised at the beginning of his submissions by referring to paragraph 13 of the decision of the Court of Appeal in the case of Angela Cannings.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: He read the paragraph out and I'll read it again if I may:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Reverting to the two possible approaches posed in a case like this in a criminal prosecution, we have no doubt that what we have described as a second approach is correct. Whether there are one, two or even three deaths, the exclusion of currently known natural causes of infant death does not establish that the death or deaths resulted from the deliberate infliction of harm. That represents not only the legal principle, which must be applied in any event, but in addition, as we shall see, at the very least it appears to us to coincide with the views of a body of expert medical opinion."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: What my learned friend didn't do is to move on to the next paragraph, which I will read at least in part:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "As we have already emphasised, the question in this case was whether there were any crimes at all and whether there were, in the legal sense, any victims of crime. As we shall see, there was no direct evidence and very little indirect evidence to suggest that they were. There was further evidence which tended to suggest that they were not."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So that is an enormous difference to the context of our case.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In our case we have 17 children, not one, two or even three. We have 22 events with which Lucy Letby was intimately associated, all of which, according to the prosecution medical evidence, are unexplained by any possible natural event. But more importantly, we have two cases in which children were poisoned with insulin, and poisoned via bags of TPN or dextrose, which Lucy Letby certainly handled.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So far as [Baby F] was concerned, it was a bag put up at 00.25 on 5 August that was poisoned and she was the person that put it up.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So far as [Baby L] was concerned, she had hung the original bag, which had nothing in it other than its legitimate contents, and at some time between just after midnight on the day she came in on that Saturday morning and the blood sample being taken towards the end of the morning, somebody deliberately put insulin into the bag.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The second bag that was hung for [Baby M] was poisoned as well and that was done at a time when Lucy Letby was there.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So just pausing there, my Lord, and moving back to paragraph 14 of Cannings, what we have here is a case in which there is very real evidence that the woman in the dock is the poisoner, and one has to look at all the other events in that context. That is something which has been singularly ignored by the defence in all the submissions they have made.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: But it doesn't end there because [Baby O] was assaulted and he was assaulted at a time when Lucy Letby was his designated nurse. He collapsed at a time when there is no evidence at all to suggest anybody else but she was there. And he sustained liver injuries which Dr Marnerides has told the court, in no uncertain terms, can in effect only be the product of an assault.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: But even there, my Lord, it doesn't end, because his brother, his triplet brother, [Baby P], his ET tube dislodged itself at a time when he was paralysed with pancuronium and when [Dr B] and [Dr A] were in the tea room at 12.28 on 24 June 2016. Yet again, Lucy Letby was the designated nurse, Lucy Letby was standing over him when it happened.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And of course, in that context, the jury will bear in mind that [Baby K]'s ET tube found its way, displaced at a time when Lucy Letby was not his designated nurse but the designated nurse had left about 2 minutes earlier, and when it was discovered who was standing over him but Lucy Letby, what was she doing?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Absolutely nothing, in a situation in which the uncontroverted expert nursing evidence was agreed and the uncontroverted evidence suggests that what she was not doing was utterly unacceptable.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So from assaults and poisonings on five children, we have the context for everything that follows and that is the context on which this jury will interpret evidence given by a large number
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: of doctors that all these other children collapsed, some of them died, for unfathomable reasons.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So my Lord, this case is completely removed from the authorities which my learned friend has quoted. There is very powerful evidence that Lucy Letby has repeatedly attacked neonates in the Countess of Chester Hospital, and she's confessed to it because she has written notes saying, "I killed them. I am evil".
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In interview she was asked why she did that and she said it's because her competencies had been challenged, but yesterday we heard from Eirian Lloyd Powell, who was present at the meeting when she in effect was moved, and she used a very emotive word to describe the way Lucy Letby reacted to being moved: it was distraught.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The type of word that most people listening to the evidence in this case would understand being used as an adjective for the parents of these children, but seems out of place, we respectfully submit, to describe the reaction of somebody who was "only" told that she would have to redo her competencies. The reason she was distraught, of course, is because, as Eirian Lloyd Powell told us, she knew she was being accused of having killed these children. It was not her competencies that were being brought into question.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: If the jury accepts that evidence from Eirian Lloyd Powell, they will reject Lucy Letby's explanation for her reasoning behind writing, "I killed them". That, my Lord, is quintessentially a matter for the jury. And to suggest, as the defence do, that this is a prosecution that rests solely on the opinions of several doctors that some of these children were killed by an air embolus is a gross distortion of the evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So my Lord, that is the context of this submission and that is why we respectfully submit it is ill-judged, to use a phrase that was used of our counter-submissions.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: My Lord, that's the starting point for our response.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I understand that some of the suggestions that we have made in writing are resented. The reason that we have set out in writing at paragraph 2 of our response our understanding of what the submission is about is to put into context the body of our response. And our understanding is that the defence seek to persuade the court that there's no case to answer on counts 1, 2, 4 and 16 because of deficiencies in the air embolus material as it stands at the conclusion of the prosecution case.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I must say, and I'm sure that it's a reflection of my inadequacies rather than the way my learned friend wrote his
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: submissions and argued them this morning, I still don't really understand the basis of the submission to this extent. One of the things my learned friend said earlier, and it's at paragraph 24 (sic) of the running [draft] transcript that we've got going, is:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "I'm not arguing admissibility."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, if the defence are not arguing admissibility, what are they arguing here?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: It may be that I have -- I'm quite prepared to accept that I have misunderstood what has been said.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Sorry, just give me a moment.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (Pause)
Please continue.

In the context of admissibility we understood -- and again I invite correction at a point where I can deal with it if I need to deal with it -- but we had understood that one of the fundamental principles of the submission was that there was -in effect, air embolus as an area of bogus science. It's what I've called "the sufficiently reliable scientific basis point".
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I don't think Mr Myers is actually suggesting it's a bogus science. That's why I asked him specifically the question: do you accept that there is a respectable -- I didn't put it this way, but there's a respectable body of medical opinion that air emboluses can cause collapses and death essentially? And Mr Myers accepts that. So air embolus itself as a mechanism for collapse and death is not controversial.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right, isn't it, Mr Myers?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Good.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So we're beyond that stage. What, as I understand it, Mr Myers is saying is that the evidence before the jury in this case from the prosecution expert witnesses is insufficient for a jury safely to conclude that in these identified counts air embolus was capable of being a cause of death.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, well, that gives rise to two issues.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: First, is that right per se? And secondly, if it is right, what's the consequence? For reasons that I've hinted at but haven't and can't today expand on in great detail, simply because of the pressure of time, we respectfully submit that there is a raft of evidence in the four counts that have been referred to -- it's [Baby A], [Baby B], [Baby D] and [Baby M] -there's a raft of evidence to support the cases against them.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So just in effect dealing with one of those cases, ex improviso, with [Baby M] we go back to [Baby L], of course, [Baby L] being poisoned. We would say there is clear evidence from which the jury could safely infer that the poisoner was Lucy Letby, and [Baby M] collapsed when, surprise, surprise, Lucy Letby had just had access to his intravenous lines.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In the context of an air embolus case, that fact in itself, when a child is exhibiting signs which the medics who are there are saying, "We have never seen before, save in some of the cases, in other cases in this particular trial", that in itself is evidence from which a jury could reasonably infer that, first of all, Lucy Letby is responsible and, secondly, the mechanism by which she achieved the collapse of the child.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: That, of course, chimes -- and moving away from [Baby M] back to [Baby A] at the beginning of June 2015 -- it chimes with evidence that the jury heard yesterday from the interviews, from the overarching interviews, in which Lucy Letby was asked about air embolus and, we would say, she feigned ignorance. And the evidence that she feigned ignorance is the fact that she had undertaken an educational course a couple of weeks earlier, and we have the record or at least part of the record of the course, in which, in her handwriting, signed and dated by her, she has identified that particular issue as being a risk with access to intravenous lines. So the jury in those circumstances, for example, would be entitled to say, "We are quite sure that she wasn't telling the truth in the interview".
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Why, if this wasn't a case of air embolus, would she possibly want to lie about her knowledge about air embolus? And the answer, of course, is to distance herself from what went on.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Just returning to the written submissions if I can, please, my Lord, we respectfully submit that many of the -- except insofar as they establish what in effect are trite principles of law, many of these authorities aren't going to assist the court in determining the particular issues that need to be resolved today.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Holdsworth, ironically, is similar to Cannings because there there was positive evidence that militated against the
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: suggestion that the defendant had committed a crime against the deceased child. We have isolated that in our paragraph 4(a)(iii). In that case the particular child in question suffered from pre-existing brain abnormalities, which predisposed him to the very sort of issue that arose and resulted in his death.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: You needn't dwell on this. Each case is factspecific.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Quite.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And the important principle is that expert evidence has to be scrutinised --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: -- and at two stages. First of all, is it admissible? And we are past that stage now because it is in evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Secondly, once it is in evidence, is it of such a nature, in the context of all the evidence in the case, such that a jury could not properly safely come to the conclusion that the evidence of the expert -- that they can rely on it?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Exactly.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's really what it boils down to.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It does, my Lord. That is precisely the point we were driving at when we deal in paragraph 4(c) with the citation of the well-known case of Galbraith because the legal principles, we would submit, are being confused here in this submission.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We all know, but it's worth repeating, that the judge in a criminal trial can stop a case at the close of the prosecution case when the evidence, viewed as a whole, is weak, vague or inconsistent.
