That is not authority for the principle which my learned friend seems to be encouraging the court to adopt, which is the judge should exclude a piece, one strand of circumstantial evidence on the basis that it's weak, vague or inconsistent. We don't for a second concede that this evidence, either on an individual case basis or taken as a class of evidence, falls within that description.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Of course, just because in my old age, after all these years, I've never heard of somebody seeking to exclude evidence on that
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: basis at half time, just because I've never heard of it doesn't mean it can't be done, but I'm not sure that there's any reported authorities to suggest that this is a correct, or even permissible, way of approaching the admissibility of evidence in a trial. The evidence is in. It's for the advocates to argue for and against it and it is for the jury to put it into the balance, to assess it individually, but, more importantly, in the context of all the other evidence, and decide where the global picture takes them.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's a count-specific approach, if you like. The case-specific approach is the cross-admissibility point, which we've raised in writing. I am not going to deal with it at any great length, but in this context, given that the nature of the defence is innocent coincidence, it is classically a case in which the evidence on one count can and should be taken into account by the jury.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: That, of course, is another reason why we would submit that to approach the submission as it has been approached, namely to say the prosecution have put all their eggs in one basket, they have taken up the challenge of proving air embolus and therefore if, looking at air embolus in a vacuum, on a case-by-case basis, the court concludes that that one class of evidence is in some way deficient by measuring it against the stick of the second limb of Galbraith, to suggest that that therefore enables the court to stop a count at half time, we would respectfully submit is -well, it's an affront to the constitutional role of the jury, in effect.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The evidence is in, it is admissible, there is no unfairness to the accused. Therefore it must be weighed in the balance and your Lordship, we would respectfully submit, can't usurp the function of the jury in a two-stage process: first, by ruling out evidence that's actually in and, secondly, by then deciding that because that one strand of the circumstantial case in an individual count is in some way deficient that the whole circumstances of the case can then be ignored and the count as a whole should fail at that stage. That's why we would respectfully submit that the process that my learned friend encourages the court to take is misconceived.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We have suggested that this application is an abuse of the process of the court and we continue to do so, for two reasons. The first is that there is material on which it is clear that this was within the contemplation of the defence from the very beginning, that if it was a legitimate approach it is a submission that should have been made before the evidence was called, and also because of the submission that your Lordship heard back in January this year concerning the evidence of Dr Evans. There, the admissibility of his evidence was being
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: challenged and if this was properly arguable it should have been argued at that time.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Otherwise, the points that we made in our written argument relating to Dr Hall are now irrelevant because they were based on what we had understood to be one of the focuses of the submission that, in effect, air embolus was bogus science. That was the purpose of --
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, well, I'm not going to have regard to Dr Hall because it's not evidence in the case. This is a submission that there is insufficient evidence for this case to proceed, so we can forget about Dr Hall.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, of course. I'm just --
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, no, I understand. You're justifying why you referred to it.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: You needn't concern me in relation to that.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Moving on to paragraph 15 of our response, which has been, in effect, repeated orally this morning, or this afternoon, that there is no consistency as to the discolouration claimed to be indicative of air embolus, and in that context, of course, Dr Bohin's evidence was referred to, we submit that's a non-point, not least because there are all sorts of articles saying all sorts of things about discolouration in air embolus.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's not only Lee and Tanswell that's been referred to in the context of this case, but just putting that to one side or putting the other articles to one side for a moment, Lee and Tanswell has two important -- a number of important points, but two points are that even in that article there are two versions of the discolouration that are seen in air embolus.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The second is the point that I think your Lordship, or it may have been my learned friend, referred to earlier, that in many cases there is no visible cutaneous sign at all. So to rely on the fact that there have been conflicting or different, rather than conflicting different, descriptions of what witnesses have seen at various stages, to rely on that as evidence that undermines a suggestion that these are cases of air embolus doesn't actually measure up to the peer-reviewed learning.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The real point, we would submit, coming out of all these discolouration episodes is that so far as the medical and nursing staff are concerned, they all say, "I've never seen anything like it before and I've never seen anything like it
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: since", except in some cases, just taking as an example [Nurse A] with [Babies A & B], where she says of [Baby B] on 9 June, "I had actually seen that about 24 hours earlier with [Baby A]".
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We submit that the essence of the air embolus type discolouration is the one that has been stressed by many of the medical practitioners: it's transient and often it's migratory and there is no -- I think it may have been Dr Gibbs or Dr Jayaram, I can't remember off the top of my head, I'm afraid, but one of them said that there is no naturally occurring illness or disease that produces visible signs like that.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And yet again, we submit, that is evidence from which a jury could infer, given what they understand about the mechanics of air embolus, the physiological characteristics of it in the sense of the air bubbles moving round the circulation and blocking off parts of the circulation or getting into the heart and stopping the heart, they could, given the evidence they have heard, conclude that these are cases of air embolus because that explains it, nothing else does.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The person that was there was Lucy Letby, often she had just had access to the lines, and it's documented.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Sometimes she was in a room where she had in effect no business to be and, as always, the child collapsed.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Going back, just before I forget, to a further piece of direct evidence which implicates Lucy Letby, we have what came out of her interviews about [Baby C], where having initially said that she'd had nothing to do with him, hadn't been in the room, when the police put her interviews to her -- sorry, when the police in interview put to her her text messages, first of all she accepted that she had been in the room at the time he had collapsed and at the time she had been both frustrated and angry.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So putting that also into the balance of the circumstantial case, we would respectfully submit that there is more than enough here for this jury to act on the evidence that they have heard about air embolus, to weigh it in the balance with all the other circumstances of the case and reasonably to convict Lucy Letby.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: My Lord, I don't know whether there are any specific issues that have been raised either by the defence that I have failed to address or issues that Mr Myers has raised this morning that I haven't answered or indeed issues that have occurred to your Lordship that you'd like me to assist on. But other than to say what I have said, in addition to what we have submitted in writing, I'm not sure that there's a great deal further that I
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: could contribute that will actively promote the cause that I seek.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr Myers.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Reply by MR MYERS
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Three matters to deal with in response if I may.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The first, which is not novel, but just to emphasise a point, is that the basis for this submission is absolutely plain and set out in our application.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It's plain because it's written there. Paragraph 7 makes it plain this is an application that there is no case to answer on counts 1, 2, 4 and 16 on the basis that your Lordship articulated by way of explanation.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And that's right, it has nothing to do with admissibility and nowhere here does it say that it does.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Paragraph 8 dealt with the position on those counts where air embolus had featured in the evidence, as to which our submission was that if we are correct in our principal submission, there would have to be a direction to the jury, we say, to disregard that evidence or deal with it however the court saw fit.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: But there's nothing novel, as it happens, in a court being required to deal with evidence that, with hindsight, is reviewed as evidence that the jury should not have. That wouldn't be a novel situation.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So we're not creating a new jurisdiction, fresh law, in asking the court to hear an application that there is no case to answer. That's plainly what it is and we could not make this application if we hadn't had all the evidence that we've had in this trial.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I pause just to remind myself of the transcripts before your Lordship, which are only a fraction of this evidence, many of which occurred both well after the start of the case, obviously, and after our application concerning Dr Evans.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We are in this position now because of the totality of the evidence and it really, we submit, isn't right to criticise the defence for making an application they are entitled to.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Well, you are entitled to make the application.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Whether it succeeds or not is for me to decide but you are not in principle prevented from making the application both of no case in relation to those counts you submit there is no case to answer and to invite me to direct the jury to disregard evidence if I came to a particular conclusion. That's within my power. It may be unusual in the circumstances but I don't think it's beyond my powers.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Not at all and we're grateful for that. It really isn't, thank you, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So we needn't worry about that.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Just two other matters then.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Certainly.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The first of those is the question of the totality of the allegations and how one impacts upon another. We recognise this may be a matter for further consideration at a certain stage, but it was an opening matter by my learned friend in which he identified five, as I recall, particulars cases, and said that in effect they set the context for this case and this should be reviewed in the light of that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So far as my note goes, none of those in fact deal with this discrete issue on counts 1, 2, 4 and 16. As I recall, none of the cases he cited were those cases.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It is something the court, we respectfully observe, may have to grapple with in due course, the relationship between the different counts on this indictment, but what we say at this point is that there are multiple factors and issues in play across these counts. This is not a case where there is such a symmetry, such a factual symmetry across the counts that what goes for one will necessarily go for all.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Taking the simplest of illustrations, a string of robberies or a string of sexual offences often exhibit precisely the same characteristics. That arguably is an easy one and it's possible there to move from what is proved on one to being of general application.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: In this case there are very different issues across the counts. In some issues there are questions of the quality of medical care generally, on some of them there are questions of the extent to which natural or clinical problems may have impacted upon what took place.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: There's not one that applies to everything. And then of course the mechanisms themselves that are alleged are different.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So we submit that we're back, in answer to that, with a fundamental submission we make, which is that on the counts of air embolus the medical evidence is and remains central to them and if the theory or the basis in terms of scientific knowledge for alleging air embolus is insufficiently reliable so that, for instance, that evidence should not be there at all, if one then considers where would those counts be without that evidence, we submit there would be no case on them, no matter what one saw elsewhere on this indictment.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So at this stage our submission is that it is no answer to the submission we make to seek to go to other counts and talk about the strength of them.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The final matter, the reasoning behind which is similar, is the question of those general factual issues, examples of which the prosecution have given, like what is in the notes and what may lie behind the notes and how they may be of general probative application and are matters to consider alongside the medical evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It was put this way, that matters like that, matters like what Eirian Powell had to say or explanations for the notes, or maybe what's said in interview, are quintessentially for the jury. Of course matters like that are and the jury will have to also weigh up the medical evidence. But the theoretical and scientific basis for that medical evidence in itself is not a matter for the jury, that's why the experts come, to explain their opinion, and the basis for that opinion and the jury can evaluate it.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: But the medical evidence, if the court forms the view that it is fundamentally unreliable or insufficiently reliable, if on that basis, again, one were to remove that from the equation where it applies, we submit that whatever questions may quintessentially be for a jury with the remaining shreds of evidence in the case or pieces of evidence, they would not be able to provide a basis of guilt where, for example, on these particular counts, air embolus is alleged. They really wouldn't be.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: There is no way of getting from a note, with what the prosecution would say is an admission on it, that could apply to any, if it is, any one of the matters on this indictment but no one in particular. There is no way of getting from that to saying: well, that that now becomes generally applicable to everything in answer to the submission that we make. Whatever its relevance, it may have nothing whatsoever to do with the counts under consideration by the court right now, and that's
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: why we say that it is the medical evidence that remains central to these and, where that is not strong enough to meet the requirements of scientific evidence, and we submit it isn't, then those counts that rely on this area of the evidence are not strong enough to go to the jury, for the reasons we have submitted.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So those are the matters we raise unless there's anything else I can assist with, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: No, thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I shall consider the respective submissions. What I'm going to do is to break off now and sit again at 2.05, by which time I will have reached my decision or decisions. But I will then announce what my decision is and then provide reasons for my decision in writing at a later time rather than trying to give an ex tempore judgment, but address the matters in some detail. Not exhaustive detail, but in some detail, in writing --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We understand, my Lord, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: -- in due course. So what I would like to do so then is, after I have done that, we will then move on to the issue in relation to the -- your representations so far as arrangements for the defendant giving evidence are concerned. We'll address those at 2.05 or 2.06. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Can the press be provided with copies of your ruling?
blocks.speaker: MEMBER OF THE PRESS

blocks.text: Certainly, you will do. But you're not going to get it today. You'll know what the decision is and I will say, "For reasons that will be put into writing", and you will be provided with copies. Certainly you should have copies. But of course it's not material that can be published at all until the conclusion of the trial. By then, a lot else will have happened. Thank you very much. You may rest assured in that regard.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much. 2.05.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The short adjournment)
Yes, Mr Myers -- do you want to say something?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No, I apologise my Lord, I was ready to deal with something else, but of course I shall wait for a moment.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. For reasons that I shall put into writing and distribute next week, I refuse the applications, the two linked applications that are made in relation to the submission of no case to answer and giving directions to the jury to ignore the expert evidence in relation to air embolus on the other counts.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: As I say, it'll be set out in detail in writing.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We understand that, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Housekeeping

So thank you again, I know I've already acknowledged your document that you provided on 4 April, actually, dated 4 April, Mr Myers. As I indicated to you yesterday, I am basically content with the proposals. Perhaps we should just go through them one by one.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes. If I may just, by way of preliminaries, set out a little bit, just very briefly, about the basis but not the detail of that that as set out in the report, just to introduce it, my Lord, if I may.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We are grateful for the court's reception of this and we're grateful to the court, I should say, for the assistance throughout the case, so far as Ms Letby and her attendance and her conduct in the trial has been concerned, and we're also most grateful to the cell staff, accompanying her to and from court. They have had a significant part to play in assisting with the process.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We know the court understands that from every perspective Ms Letby has to be able to deal with the evidence as well as she is capable and we've set out the material we rely upon, I don't go through that now, it's in the report.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: When we come to consider the arrangements, the only matters that I advert to specifically are concerns as to what's described as hypervigilance and hypersensitivity to aspects of her surroundings. That's something that we are concerned with and we know the court will seek to assist us with and Ms Letby with to ensure there is no disruption from that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Again, being careful not to go beyond where I need to for what we're dealing with here, to monitor closely how she deals with the process that she is going to be dealing with, which on any view would be a demanding process for anybody, and there
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: certainly is material to indicate a marked degree of -potential degree of fragility. So we're most anxious that that be monitored closely because of the potential for significant problems in certain circumstances. I don't go into more detail than that because I know that your Lordship has the submissions and the material that goes with them.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Which I have obviously read and take account of.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Having set that out, can I go through the measures, just to deal with them -- and in fact, if I may, can I deal with what appears at the end because it's something that, as it stands there, may cause more or may potentially cause more concern than would be necessary. That's (x) and (xi) at the end of paragraph 33, which refers to contact with legal representatives during the giving of evidence. May I put the court's mind at rest as to where that lies because that would be a most extraordinary course to take.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It's not one that, at the outset, we are seeking at all, but your Lordship will see the paragraph that follows that talks about contingencies and having in mind any issues that may develop. And bearing in mind the material that we had received by way of reports and what had been said, it seemed appropriate just to raise the issue for the court in terms of forewarning it and monitoring how the defendant is as to what may be required in extremis or depending upon the way events go.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: But it's not something we would seek to persuade the court needs to take place now and if we try to, we anticipate it would probably be unsuccessful, so we don't.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That was the only one that stuck out in my mind. It would be wholly exceptional. But I understand exactly what you're saying: we needn't go into it because you know what I'm saying, I know what you're saying. Should particular circumstances arise then consideration can be given to how to address those circumstances.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That's why I went there first.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Exactly. That's absolutely fine.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: But then you proceed as you wish to in relation to the remainder.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The first point that we ask the court to consider, and it's something your Lordship's made reference to already, is the
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: sessions of evidence and breaks enabling the defendant to cope with the demands of giving evidence. As to that, there is a matter that I have been informed of via the cell staff, for which I'm grateful. It's this: that in fact breaks that are longer than 15 minutes are very -- will result in the defendant then having to be taken downstairs, with various arrangements that have to be made because of her categorisation, which can in fact be more disruptive or less helpful maybe than a break of about 15 minutes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Right. I understand that. It doesn't surprise me. It also means that, as I understand it, she would then be essentially in the back of the court and in a safe space --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: -- and not coming into contact with anyone else and not wasting time going up and down and so on and so forth. So fifteen-minute breaks then.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That would be helpful. Then the defendant is within the area of the court, albeit just outside the court, and it's less disruptive.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: What I'm going to say to, Mr Johnson, is if you wish to contribute to any of the proposals at any time feel free to do so. But fifteen-minute -- a mid-morning fifteen-minute break and a mid-afternoon fifteen-minute break.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We can see how matters proceed, but I'd ask your Lordship to consider whether the evidence could be kept within about hour blocks, as we move along. We can monitor that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, exactly. I'm not sticking rigidly to the exact hour, but as we do conventionally, either just slightly under the hour if it's a convenient point to break or slightly over the hour. But basically, two one-hour sessions in each half of the day.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, thank you, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Just pausing there, when dealing with arrangements and the custody element, from the cell staff there will be arrangements necessary for the moving to and fro in court. One matter that it occurs to us is necessary to consider is whether the defendant is in position before, for instance, the public are in court. A bit like the screens being put up and taken down. It may well be a matter that the court has already considered or been asked to consider.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. I think the answer is going to be yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Well, I don't go into that any further at this point but --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So that will have to be factored in.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Rather like the screens, in other words.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Exactly, yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Very well, thank you, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: In other words, the court will be closed until a point when everyone can come into court.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I will address that specifically next week.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The second matter -- in fact originally we'd asked whether the defendant may have, in fact, papers copies of the sequence of events charts. Having considered the matter further, in fact very recently, the request we would make is whether she can simply take the iPad that she has used. Having used the A3 files myself and knowing I will be using them, they can be quite cumbersome with a good deal of space around and it may be less help than more help to deal with those. But if the defendant could have use of the iPad in the course of the evidence, then if it is necessary for her to refer to whatever is being dealt with, she can, if that creates no impediment.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I'll just check first with Mr Johnson.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Absolutely no objection.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'm then going to check with the senior officer. Will that be acceptable? All right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We're grateful, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: She can rest assured she will have access to an iPad.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The next two matters, items 3 and 4, I approach with appropriate circumspection because they deal with the way that the evidence is approached and obviously a particular view as to how my learned friend or the prosecution deal with it. It's not
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: something I elaborate upon here because I recognise it's unnecessary for me to do so, but I leave it with the court and my learned friend, and of course we shall see how the defendant is. But I simply ask that it be kept in mind, from whatever angle we approach the evidence, it is a huge task to deal with, the evidence in this case. She'll be the only witness who will give evidence in the length and for the variety of areas that she will do, and with that in mind, we ask that it be approached in a way that does accommodate that difficulty or that challenge, let me put it that way.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We appreciate the difference between how questions have to be for the purpose they are designed to serve and the point at which potentially there may be issues that are entirely collateral to the main purpose of questioning. We leave it to the court and my learned friend for that to be kept in mind, as it would with any witness.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Well, I will certainly, obviously, keep a very close eye on her whilst she's giving evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm sure we can rely on Mr Johnson when it comes to --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I state publicly, there is no value to the prosecution in confusing anybody.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Absolutely. If I think there is any confusion or it's apparent that the witness is tiring and needs a break, I will just intervene at that point.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We don't regard it as necessary for us to elaborate upon that, but we just state it for the reassurance of all.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The next two matters which I identify and which is the movement around the courtroom is really a matter we leave with your Lordship. The arrangements to be made for the way the court will sit with the defendant has already been considered. It's always undesirable for there to be unnecessary movement in and out of court and we simply observe there are aspects of Ms Letby's condition which, we submit on the basis of the material we have, make her uniquely sensitive to noises, movements, things that distract or unsettle. That will probably become apparent when she gives her evidence, but we ask that there be as little interruption around her as possible. That would be the case anyway but it is likely to be more disruptive here than it might in other cases.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It's always very distracting in any event whenever anyone is giving evidence when there's movement in and out of the court. And you will have seen for the months that we're all been together that the usher has been absolutely
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: fastidious, if someone wants to come into court, about going and addressing them. He will do that as well and continue to do that. So it will be made plain that people -- I won't be having coming and going and if people want to leave, they'll leave for the rest of the session.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We're grateful to Mr Stansfield, of course.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It has been, in fact, apart from when someone's had a coughing fit and has had to go, it has been very well ordered and will continue to be very well ordered.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We are grateful, my Lord. Item 7 I can raise with my learned friend; it perhaps doesn't need me to go into the details there. It just relates to matters which may impact upon the defendant's sense of well-being. That is item 7 on page 8. That arrangement can be made between prosecution and defence as to who sits where.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I don't think it's going to arise.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It won't because if the court is constituted once the defendant is in place, as long as she doesn't turn round to look at people, she won't see anyone.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Exactly.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: There is an issue or I was led to believe there is an issue about the screen. Is that right?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm grateful to Mr Maher, who tells me the screen will be turned off in fact.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That's what I was going to confirm. That will be done, yes. It'll be dimmed. You won't be able to see an image. All right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Item 8 makes reference to the comforters that that Ms Letby has. She would be grateful, and on her behalf we would be grateful, so long as they create no issue and we don't see how they can, that she at least has those with her. They have played a part so far at every step of the way.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Mr Johnson, anything to say to that?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, certainly she may have her comforters.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Item 9. All of these matters of important. This is a matter which is and has proved to be quite crucial with Ms Letby, that she can have contact with the court liaison and diversion lead practitioner, who has been Ms Santolini(?) to date. It has been of enormous assistance to her and, as a result of that, to us and thereafter to the court, that Ms Letby has been as able to cope with matters as she has and had the support that she has. Ms Santolini is a professional who deals with this, has been of enormous benefit to her with that, and we would be grateful, so far as it can be arranged, that contact continues, merely for the purpose of support, as it has been throughout, between Ms Letby and Ms Santolini. And so we would be grateful if your Lordship were to consider that and assent to that taking place. It doesn't involve the evidence and will not involve the evidence, it's purely for support.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Mr Johnson?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Nothing to say, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, again, I accede to that request.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I will say this to Ms Letby now and I will say it once she commences her evidence, that of course she must not talk to anyone about any of the evidence in the case, and that includes the escorting staff or Ms Santolini, once she has started her evidence. And that embargo remains in place until she has completed her evidence, which is going to be a long time. She can talk about welfare issues, obviously, but not about the evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She will understand that and will abide by that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We're grateful for those measures, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I emphasise in conclusion that, as with any defendant, but for various reasons especially for Ms Letby, the support she's had to date has been crucial in coping with the process she is going through, and the protracted and at times fragmented nature of it, as it now comes closer, will put its own strains at a time when there's perhaps less support than there has been.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So certainly we will observe very closely how matters proceed and we know the court will. And we are most grateful, as she will be, for every piece of assistance she can have to deal with what is going to take place next.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We will keep the court informed if there's any matter that causes us concern, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: As is apparent from what I have acceded to, I am obviously anxious to ensure that she is able to give her best evidence. It goes without saying that it will be a stressful time for her. I have to observe the rules of the court, and they will be observed, and I know you will have explained them all to her. They will be observed. But in relation to the matters that we've canvassed, I am quite content to assist her and therefore the trial process and therefore the interests of justice --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: -- in that way.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We're grateful for that, my Lord, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Unless there's anything else I can assist with, those are the matters we wish to raise.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you very much, Mr Myers.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Anything, Mr Johnson?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No, thank you, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Thank you very much indeed. Obviously, if anything arises you will, I know, alert me to it.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So on Tuesday, when we assemble, of course the jury will now be coming in, expecting to recommence on Tuesday morning, and then the court will sit at 10.30, barring some unforeseen circumstance arising, which it has done in the past, and then we'll take it from there.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, my Lord, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: She will know that it will just be Tuesday. Wednesday and Thursday will be rest days for her, which may not be a bad thing after the first day, and then we'll proceed thereafter.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We're grateful, my Lord, thank you. May we have the opportunity to speak with Ms Letby before we conclude today?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Certainly, as far as I'm concerned, yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The senior escorting officer, as usual, is very accommodating in that regard.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And I express my thanks for all the assistance that the court has been provided with.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Nothing else then?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord, no.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The court will therefore stand adjourned until 10.30 on Tuesday morning. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The court adjourned until 10.30 am on Tuesday, 2 May 2023)
